Since this act is usually not carried out independently except by the leaders (ru'asa'), he indicated this by his words: ﴿then fight﴾. He placed the address to the leaders in the position of their pronoun, as an incitement to fight them and an indication that they broke the oaths and proceeded to the disgrace of lying, and that they would not have considered departing from the customs of the noble (al-kiram) to be shameful unless they had already become firmly rooted in disbelief. So he said: ﴿the leaders of disbelief﴾. Then he indicated, with his words, giving the reason for the permissibility of fighting: ﴿Indeed they have no oaths﴾, that (p-392) this holds even if the followers did it and the leaders did not restrain them, since it proceeds from their collective agreement. So begin with the heads and cut them off, and the tails will be cut off.

The reading of Ibn 'Amir with the kasra (ʾinnahum la ʾaymana lahum, "indeed they have no oaths," with the kasra on the initial hamzah) means: there is no safe-conduct for them, because they have broken the covenant that required it through what has occurred from them. Whoever among the people of the dhimmah (ahl al-dhimmah, the protected non-Muslim subjects under a covenant) openly attacks Islam becomes liable to be killed, for the covenant obliges him not to attack.

Then he gave the reason for fighting with his words: ﴿so that they may desist﴾, meaning: make your aim in fighting them that their condition become that of one who desists from his error upon seeing from you sincere earnestness and a firm limit.

Al-Bukhari related in the Tafsir from Hudhayfah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "None remained of the companions of this verse except three, and none of the hypocrites except four, one of whom is an aged shaykh who, even if he drank cold water, would not find its coldness."

When He had negated their oaths by negating their faith, he began to establish proof for that with matters they had committed, each of which had a cause that moved one to confront them. He urges fighting them in the form of a wonder at those who are lax about it, so he said: ﴿Will you not?﴾ The particle *alā* (a particle of urging, *ḥarf ʿarḍ*) here means urging, because the interrogative *hamza* of denial (*hamzat al-inkār*) has entered upon the negation and so negated it, and what follows it becomes affirmed by way of urging to it. This is more eloquent than if it had been affirmed without this style. ﴿Fight a people﴾, meaning: even if they possess great strength. ﴿Who broke their oaths﴾, meaning: in the matter of ʿĀṣim and his companions, al-Mundhir and his companions, and the aiding against Khuzāʿa, and other things. (p-393) Breaking oaths was therefore a custom and a trait for them. This indicates that fighting those who break oaths is more fitting than fighting others, so that this may deter from breaking pacts.

The account of Khuzāʿa was that between them and Banū Bakr ibn ʿAbd Manāt ibn Kināna there had been killing in the Jāhiliyya. Khuzāʿa had entered into the covenant of the Prophet ﷺ at al-Ḥudaybiyya, because of the love they had for him from both their Muslims and their unbelievers, due to the alliance between them, as was mentioned at the end of al-Anfāl. Banū Bakr had entered into the covenant of Quraysh. Time passed on this, then Anas ibn Zanīm al-Dīlī satirized the Messenger of God ﷺ. A boy from Khuzāʿa heard him and attacked him, wounding his head. He went out to his people and showed them his wound, so evil erupted, along with what was already between them, and what Banū Bakr sought from Khuzāʿa of their blood. Banū Nufātha of Banū Bakr spoke to the nobles of Quraysh, and they found the people eager for that. So they aided them with weapons, mounts and men. Nawfal ibn Muʿāwiya al-Dīlī went out, and he was their leader on that day. Ibn Isḥāq said: not all of Banū Bakr pledged allegiance to him. al-Wāqidī said: Banū Mudlij withdrew and did not break the covenant. Then they attacked Khuzāʿa by night while they were at al-Watīr, a water source of theirs. They struck a man from them and went beyond limits, and they fought. Along with them fought some of Quraysh who fought by night, secretly, disguised and veiled: Ṣafwān ibn Umayya, Mikraz ibn Ḥafs ibn al-Akhyaf, Ḥuwayṭib ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā, and ʿIkrima ibn Abī Jahl. They also mobilized their slaves along with them. Khuzāʿa was secure because of the covenant and the truce.

When he reminded them of their breaking of oaths in general regarding their right, and reminded them of what they had singled out against their leader, indeed the leader of all creation, he said: ﴿And they resolved to expel the Messenger﴾, meaning: from Mecca during the ʿUmrat al-Qaḍāʾ. Indeed they ordered him to leave when the three days had ended, and they insisted on that. Although he had agreed with them on that, Ibn Isḥāq and others have related, in the account of the proclamation with Sūrat Barāʾa, that the agreement between him and them was that no one who came to the House as a visitor would be prevented. Perhaps they resolved to expel him before the three days, because of the envy that overtook them when they witnessed the vigor and numbers of his companions and their good condition. This is not far from their deeds and their open disavowal of him ﷺ, to the point that they became bold, though he is the highest of creation in rank, the most splendid in appearance and light, and the purest in traces and marks, in insisting upon his leaving the land of his fathers and forefathers, who are more entitled to it than they are, and the place of his birth and upbringing. However, I have not seen this stated explicitly. In my view, even with its own merits, it is more fitting than what they mentioned about resolving to expel him at the Emigration, as is not hidden. Or the intended meaning may be what the hypocrite Ibn Ubayy and those who followed him from among his companions resolved, namely the expulsion of the Prophet ﷺ from Medina, when he said in the expedition of al-Muraysīʿ: ﴿If we return to Medina, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it﴾ [al-Munāfiqūn: 8], after they had given pledges of shelter, support and Islam. This is to remind the believers of their hastening to breaking after he had established that they are, in joining together in the plot against Islam, like one body. It is as if He says: if these have abandoned their faith, then those are more deserving to break their oaths. This is an impulse to the believers to disavow the unbelievers, whether hypocrites or open, near or distant.

When he reminded them of treachery in general and in particular, he followed it with what confirmed it through fighting, so he said: ﴿And they began against you﴾, meaning: by agreement of their inner thoughts and outward conduct, ﴿first﴾, meaning: by fighting and obstruction at al-Ḥudaybiyya, after you had informed them that you had not come for fighting, and that you had come only as visitors to the Sacred House, in which people are equal and you are more entitled to it than they are. That is "first" in relation to this second [occasion], like His saying: ﴿You were content to sit at home the first time﴾ [al-Tawba: 83]. Some commentators said: what is meant by "first time" is their fighting of Khuzāʿa, which is clear, because it was after the conclusion of the truce. It was also said: at Badr, after their caravan was saved and they said: we will not return until we uproot Muḥammad and his companions. It was also said: what is meant is fighting in general, because the Prophet ﷺ brought them the Clear Book and called them with the utmost gentleness, and challenged them with it when they denied, so they turned away from that to fighting. Thus they (p-396) are the aggressors, and the aggressor is more unjust.

When He commanded them to fight, and fighting was hated by souls in every state, he began to explain the causes that drive one to be lax about fighting them. He restricted them to fear and affection. He divided affection into what has its cause in the nearness of good deeds, and what has its cause in kinship and marriage. He refuted all of them and explained that none of them is fit to be a cause. He began with fear, because it is the greatest cause for abandoning confrontation. He rebuked them, censuring them, so that this would be more eloquent in urging fighting them, alerting that laxity regarding them makes the description of cowardice and weakness of religion correct. He said: ﴿Do you fear them?﴾, meaning: do you fear that they would prevail over you in fighting, by being, in their falsehood, more intense than you are in your truth? ﴿Then God﴾, meaning: the One who possesses the totality of greatness, ﴿is more deserving﴾, meaning: than them, ﴿that you fear Him﴾, meaning: that He should be feared by you, because of what you know of His power in seizing whoever opposes Him, even after a long delay, ﴿if you are believers﴾, meaning: for whoever affirms that He is the One who is singular in the attributes of greatness does not look at anything other than His awe.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 9, verse 14:

When He had rebuked them for their slackness in regard to them, He promised them what would remove their fear of them, or rather would make them eager to advance against them and keen to engage them. So He stated plainly what the interrogative of reproach in ﴿Will you not fight?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 13] implied, by way of a command: ﴿Fight them﴾, that is, for the sake of Allah alone and not for any other purpose. ﴿Allah will punish them﴾, that is, the One in whom you believe to be the sole possessor of the attributes of majesty (p-397) and beauty, ﴿at your hands﴾, that is, by your killing them, taking them captive and defeating them. ﴿And He will disgrace them﴾, that is, through humiliation in this world, and shame and punishment in the Hereafter.

Since this was a statement that does not necessarily entail victory, which is the ascendancy of the outcome, He said: ﴿And will give you victory over them﴾, that is, so that you may please your Lord by it, by humbling, through you, one who opposes Him. And since their punishment in the manner mentioned would produce joy for some of the believers, in which they had a share, He made clear, exalted is He, that this does not affect the work after it has been firmly established on the foundation of sincerity. So He said: ﴿And will heal﴾, that is, by it, ﴿the breasts of a people who are believers﴾, that is, firmly rooted in faith, who had earlier done them wrongs that gave rise to resentments and grudges, such as Khuza'ah and others who had aided against them or wronged them.

When the healing is not always intended to mean complete recovery, He followed it, to confirm its completeness, with His words: ﴿and remove the rage of their hearts﴾, meaning: He establishes in their hearts, in place of what they suffered from them of hardship, the opposite pleasure, and removes from them the pain that had afflicted them, through the deed of those among their enemies whom He wills to punish, and through the humiliation of the rest. Indeed, He (glorified is He) fulfilled what He had promised, so this verse is among the clear proofs.

Since the implied sense was: "Fight them, for if you fight them, such-and-such will happen," He (glorified is He) joined to the root of this sentence His words: ﴿and Allah turns in mercy to whom He wills﴾, meaning: the King who possesses the attributes of perfection, [turns in mercy] ﴿to whom He wills﴾, meaning: from among them, so that they become your brothers and allies. The sense is: Fight them, and the fighting will be the cause of these five things. As for repentance, it is sometimes caused by fighting and sometimes by something else; and because it is possible that repentance is caused by fighting, it has been read irregularly (shadhdhan) in the accusative (bi-l-nasb), on the basis that the waw is for *sarf* (a conjunction of diversion, i.e., meaning "and then," reversing the expected sequence). Since what this true promise includes revolves around power and knowledge, and knowledge entails power, the implied sense is: "Allah is over all things capable," and He joined to it His words: ﴿and Allah﴾, meaning: He to whom belongs comprehensive encompassment of everything in knowledge and power, ﴿is Knowing﴾, meaning: of everything, and of who is fit for repentance and who is not, and of what is in your hearts of advancing and holding back, and how it would be if it came out into the external world; ﴿Wise﴾, meaning: He perfected all His affairs, and He did not tie the legal rulings concerning your acquired deeds except to what knowledge relates to in the state of its manifestation.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 9, verse 16:

Since the implied meaning was what their abstention from fighting indicates, and the interrogative particle *am* (أم), which signals that what follows it is in the middle of the speech, the beginning (*ibtida'*, the initial position) of which is only the alif (ألف) alone, the sentence is as follows: "Or do you think that He, exalted is He, does not know that, or is not able to give you victory?" On this basis He said, rebuking those who were sluggish in that matter with a kind of sluggishness: ﴿Or did you think﴾, meaning: due to a deficiency in intellect, that He would base the matter on other than wisdom. This is what is meant by His saying ﴿that you would be left﴾, meaning: remaining in what you are upon, without being tested by that which distinguishes the believer from the hypocrite. ﴿When﴾ (*lamma*, ولما) He used it because it indicates, together with the continuation of past time, that what follows it is expected to occur. ﴿Allah knows﴾, meaning: He who encompasses all attributes of perfection, ﴿those of you who strove﴾, meaning: knowledge that is manifest, by which the proof is established against you in the course of your customs according to the dictates of your intellects, by the striving occurring in reality, in fact.

Since the meaning was: strive sincerely, he translated and expanded it by His saying: ﴿and did not﴾, meaning: and when Allah has not yet known those who did not ﴿take﴾. It may be a circumstantial clause (*hal*, حال). He indicated the distance of ranks from His exalted station by His saying: ﴿other than Allah﴾, meaning: the One from whom one does not turn away and desire another, whoever has even a little insight, as the reflexive form (*ifti'al*) indicates, because He is the one singular in perfection. He emphasized the negation by repeating *la* (لا), so He said: ﴿nor His Messenger﴾, meaning: he who is the essence of His creation, ﴿nor the believers﴾, meaning: those whom He has chosen from among His servants, ﴿as an intimate (*waliyjah*, وليجة)﴾, meaning: an inner confidant with whom you conceal matters and whom you trust, so that your secrets enter into them and their secrets into you. The *waliyjah* is anything you insert into something that is not part of it. A man may be among a people without being one of them, and so his *waliyjah* is the one he singles out with the innermost matters of his affairs apart from people. It is said: "He is my *waliyjah*," and "They are my *waliyjah*," used for both the singular and the plural. Al-Baghawi transmitted this from Abu 'Ubaydah. Ibn Hisham said: *waliyjah* means an intimate (*dakhil*), and its plural is *walai'j*. He says: they did not take an intimate other than Him, to whom they confide what they do not show, like what the hypocrites do: they show faith to those who believe (p-400), and when they are alone with their devils they say: "Indeed, we are with you."

The conclusion is that abstention cannot occur without both matters being present as knowledge, and the intended meaning of negating knowledge is negating the thing known. So the meaning is: there are not yet strivers who are sincere.

Since the apparent meaning of this is a likely occasion for one whose foothold in the knowledge of the realities is not firm to cling to it, He concluded with His saying: ﴿And Allah﴾, meaning: He to whom belongs complete encompassing, ﴿is Aware of what you do﴾, meaning: whether it comes out into the open or not.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 9, verse 17:

When He had warned them against taking an intimate (*waliyja*) other than Him, he began to make clear that the intimacy which some of them take is not suitable for the bond of kinship, because of the good deeds with which it is characterised, as long as those good deeds are not placed on the foundation, which is faith, made manifest by its proofs. So he said, leading into it as an answer to someone who had said: "Indeed, among them are acts of goodness that call for leaving them alone, such as building up the Sacred Mosque, serving it, and honouring it!" ﴿It is not for the polytheists﴾. He expressed it with the description rather than the verb, because a group of those who associated partners with Allah later became Muslim, and so became fit for what was negated of them. ﴿to maintain the mosques of Allah﴾, that is, the One who is exalted above all deficiency by His encompassing all attributes of perfection. Al-Baghawi said: Al-Hasan said: "It is not for the polytheists that they be left to become the people of the Sacred Mosque." Then he said, in explaining the reading in the plural: Al-Hasan said: "He only said *masajid Allah* (the mosques of Allah) because it is the qibla of all mosques," meaning that whoever maintains it maintains all the mosques. It is also possible that the intended sense is the genus (*jins*), and when they are not fit to maintain the genus, the Sacred Mosque is included, because it is the foremost of the genus; and this is more emphatic because it is by way of metonymy (*kinaya*). Al-Farra' said: "Often the Arabs treat the singular as plural and the plural as singular. Do you not see that a man rides a *birdhawn* (a horse of inferior breed) and says, 'I have taken to riding the *baradhin* (horses of inferior breed)'; and it is said, 'So-and-so has much *dirham* and *dinar*'?" End of quote.

Thus it becomes clear that the meaning is: preventing them from performing the rites of Allah, whether by circumambulation, visitation, or otherwise, because they are impure, as will come.

﴿bearing witness against themselves﴾, that is, their selves, which are the source of filth and desires, ﴿with disbelief﴾, that is, by their own confession; because it is the House of Allah, and they worship other than Allah, and they have set up idols in it without His permission and claimed that they are His partners. So permitting their maintenance of it is a ruin, since it contradicts their creed and their action. Al-Baghawi said: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "Their witness was their prostration to the idols. That is because they had set up their idols outside the Sacred House, near the foundations, and they used to circumambulate the House naked; whenever they completed a circuit (*shawt*), they prostrated to their idols."

When he had negated the ugliness of what they do, he pointed to their distance from good by saying: ﴿Those, their deeds have failed﴾, that is, the deeds of maintenance, keeping of the keys (*hijaba*), providing water to pilgrims (*siqaya*), and other things; they were ruined through the nullification of their meanings, because they were built on something other than a foundation. ﴿And in the Fire they will abide﴾, that is, they specifically, and whoever does as they did is among them, ﴿forever﴾ (p-402), that is, because they made disbelief in place of faith.

When he had negated their fitness for maintaining (al-'imarah), he explained who is fit for it, saying: ﴿Only he maintains the mosques of God﴾. That is, only one who is qualified for that nearness is one who possesses the Most Beautiful Names and the Highest Attributes, [who maintains them] physically through purifying the self, and in meaning through glorifying them with acts of worship, by cleaning and sweeping them, repairing what has collapsed, and illuminating them with physical lamps, and with spiritual illumination through remembrance (dhikr) and recitation, the teaching of knowledge ('ilm) being the most excellent of these, and by guarding them from what they were not built for, namely worldly talk. ﴿Who believes in God﴾, that is, the King on High, to whom all affairs belong, ﴿and the Last Day﴾. That is, he is among the people of true knowledge (ma'rifah) whose worship is sound and beneficial to them, for it benefits only on that Day. He did not mention belief in the Messenger, because this disavowal (bara'ah) was taken from his tongue, so belief in it is necessarily belief in him, and therefore omitting his mention is more forceful in making belief in him obligatory. ﴿And establishes the prayer and gives the zakat﴾. That is, he confirms his claim of faith with these two witnesses. This is because maintaining the mosques is not an end in itself; rather it is a sign of the firmness of faith. The prayer is the greatest of their maintenance, and zakat is what aids the foundation of their maintenance.

Since it might be understood from his saying ﴿believes﴾ that mere verbal affirmation suffices for faith, he informed us that it is necessary in this matter to bring about true assent (tasdiq), which yields the fear of God. Therefore he said: ﴿and fears none but God﴾. That is, in religious acts, ﴿and fears none but God﴾ (p-٤٠٣), that is, he does not act upon the requirement of fearing anyone other than the Supreme King, by refraining from what pleases God in fear of what displeases someone else, but rather he prefers what God's pleasure is confined to, even if it entails his own destruction. The summary of this is that he gives precedence to his fear of God over his fear of others. This returns to His saying: ﴿God has more right that you should fear Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 13]. However, this is more eloquent, because it negates the very fear itself, even though what is intended is the negation of its customary concomitant. In this there is a rebuke to them, that they are not fit to serve Him, because they fear the idols and perform with them acts of worship in the manner of one who fears them.

When he had established, by negation and affirmation, that one who possesses these attributes is deserving of guidance and worthy of it, the Exalted said: ﴿Perhaps those will be among the rightly guided (al-muhtadin)﴾. That is, those of high aspirations (al-'aliyu al-himam), ﴿will be﴾, that is, by innate disposition and firm establishment, ﴿among the rightly guided﴾. Thus, along with what was previously mentioned of perfection in knowledge and deeds, He placed them between hope and fear, with the indication, by singling out "fear," of the preference of fear over hope, as an announcement of the exaltedness of His command and the immensity of His greatness, indicating that no one has any right over Him, that if He wills He rewards, and if He wills to judge, He—being the Just Judge—decides punishment, and He is not questioned about what He does. He repeated the Greatest Name (al-ism al-a'zam) to increase the encouragement, given the gravity of the station and the nobility of the goal. The root of ʿasā (perhaps), in all its conjugations, revolves around motion, and this particular form is for inspiring hope. The summary is that whoever possesses the four attributes is fit, suitable, deserving and worthy that his hope be stirred and his expectation extended to becoming one of the people of guidance. So how can you, then, make obligatory for one who lacks any one of these what is specific to the rightly guided, namely, loyalty (al-muwalah)? (p-٤٠٤) Thus it appeared to me first in the basic root's context, and then it appeared to me that this holds in most of its permutations, while it is possible that something else is meant for removal, and that what encompasses them all, whether with yaʾ or waw as the radical, in its ten permutations: ʿasā, ʿaysa, saʿā, yasaʿa, ʿasawa, ʿawasa, saʿawa, sawaʿa, wasiʿa, and ʿasa, is that they apply to what may occur, and what is deserving and fitting to occur, from the expression "aʿissa bihi," meaning: "it is fitting for him" (akhliq).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 9, verse 18 (part 2 of 3):

*ʿasā* (عسى) also means *bi-al-ḥariyy* (بِالحَرِيِّ), "it is likely/deserving," that he will do something. And *innahu la-maʿsāh bi-kadhā* (إنَّهُ لَمَعْساةٌ بِكَذا) means "he is fit/shaped for such-and-such" (*makhlaqah*, "fit for it"). Sibawayh explained it in this sense. Ibn Hisham al-Khadrawi said in his commentary on Abu ʿAli's *Sharḥ al-Īḍāḥ*: Sibawayh said that *ʿasā* is in the position of *ikhlawlaqa* (اخْلَوْلَقَ, "to be fit/likely"). *Al-miʿsāʾ*, like *mikhsāl*, is a girl who has reached puberty, because she is fit to accept marriage. For this reason it (*ʿasā*) is used for hope and apprehension. Hope may increase and be applied to nearness, so it is like *kāda* (كادَ, "to be about to"). It may also become strong and reach certainty, and then we use it in the sense of *kāna* (كانَ, "was"). From this is the saying *ʿasā al-Ghuwayr abʾusan* (عَسى الغُوَيْرُ أبْؤُسًا, "perhaps al-Ghuwayr will bring misfortunes"). However, al-Radi said: "I do not know *ʿasā* used for certainty except in the speech of God, the Exalted." Hope may also weaken and become doubt, and from this is *al-muʿsiyah* (المُعْسِيَةُ), like *muḥsinah*, for a she-camel: it is doubtful whether she has milk or not.

*ʿasiya al-nabāt* (عَسِيَ النَّباتُ), in the pattern of *faraḥa* and *daʿā*, means the plant became thick and dried, i.e., it became fit to be grazed and to be cut. Likewise *al-yad min al-ʿamal* (the hand from work) has the same form, i.e., the hand became fit to endure hardships. *Al-ʿāsī* is the palm tree, because it is fit to give all the benefits that are sought from it. *ʿAsiya al-shaykh* (عَسِيَ الشَّيْخُ), like *raḍiya*, *ʿasāʾan* and *ʿasan* like *daʿā*, *yaʿsū*, means he became old, i.e., he became fit for death and for not learning what was not in his nature. Similarly, *ʿasā* and *ʿasā al-insān ʿan al-adab* means he grew too old for it. *Al-ʿūd* (the stick) dried, became hard and firm, i.e., became fit for what is intended from it. *Al-layl* (the night): its darkness intensified, so it became fit for its name to match what it names and for covering matters. *Al-ʿusuww* is wax, as if, by removing the darkness of the night with its light, it burns. *ʿAsiya bi-al-shayʾ* like *faraḥa* means he was bound to it, i.e., he became fit to be attached to it. *Al-ʿayn* (with fatḥah) is the stallion's mating; it is said that its water (is so called) because it is fit for producing offspring. *Al-ʿīs* (with kasrah) are white camels in which a reddish tint mixes with the whiteness. A camel or a gazelle is *aʿyas*, and a she-camel is *ʿayṣāʾ*, because she is fit for every praise because of the beauty of her color. *Ta ʿayyasat al-ibil* means the camels became white amid blackness, likewise. *ʿAyṣāʾ* is also a woman's name, and the female locust is so called because of its resemblance to the color of *al-ʿīs*. *Aʿyasa al-zarʿ* (the crop became *aʿyas*) when there was no moisture in it, because it became fit for harvest. *Al-ʿaws* (with fatḥah) and *al-ʿawasān* mean roaming at night, because it is fit to reach its goals. (p-406) With ḍammah, *al-ʿawsī* is a kind of sheep, and it is a ram *ʿawsī*. It is linked to *al-ʿīs* but, because of its small size, ḍammah was chosen for it to compensate for it, to strengthen it, and as a good omen of growth. For camels kasrah was chosen as a good omen of easy leading. With fatḥah and sukūn, *al-ḥaraka* is the movement of the two jaws at laughter or otherwise, by analogy with sheep; so it is as if it is fit to leave off what happens from it, such as laughter and other things. The adjective is *aʿwas* and *ʿawsāʾ*. *ʿAsa ʿalā ʿiyālihi* means he toiled for them and strove; *ʿiyālahu* means he supported them. *Mālahu ʿawsan* and *ʿiyāsatan* mean he managed it well, doing what was most fitting for it in all that. *Al-ʿuwāsah* with ḍammah is a sip of milk or other drink, because it is fit to quench thirst. *Al-aʿwas* is the polished one and the one who describes a thing, because it is fit to reveal what is hidden. *Al-ʿawsāʾ*, like *burākāʾ*, is a pregnant female beetle; in that state it is more fit for what its root conveys of aversion, for it is said *khanfasa ʿan al-qawm* (خَنْفَسَ عَنِ القَوْمِ), meaning he disliked them and turned away from them. *Al-khunāfis* with ḍammah is the lion, because it is fit to be disliked and avoided. *Al-saʿy* is running below full speed, and every work is *saʿy*. Al-Qamus said: *saʿā* like *raʿā* means he intended, knew, walked, ran, gained, and each of these is fit to attain one's need. *Al-siʿāyah* is the direct handling of the work of charity by which the ruler obtains the rights (due), so it is fit to enrich the poor. *Saʿati al-ummah* means she (the female slave) committed fornication, so she was fit for the work of maidservants among the Arabs. *Sāʿāhā* means he sought her for prostitution. *Asʿāhu* means he made him run. *Al-masʿāh* is nobility and high status in kinds of glory, because it is fit that one strives for it. *Istasʿā al-ʿabd* means he assigned to the slave work by which he would pay for himself when part of him was freed, so that he could free the rest, because he is fit for that. *Al-siʿāyah* with kasrah is what is assigned from that. *Al-saysʿ* is water flowing on the surface of the earth, and *insāʿa* means it flowed, because water is fit for flowing and movement. *Sāʿa al-māʾ wa-al-sharāb* means it moved over the surface of the earth. *Sayʿāʾ* from the night and *kasayrāʾ* are pieces of it, as if one looks at the hour, which is a part that, because of its preciousness, is fit to be guarded, not wasted, and to be made up for if wasted. *Al-sayyāʿ* with fatḥah is what is plastered with, and fat with which a waterskin is smeared, as if it prevents what is fit to flow. I have *sayyaʿtu al-jubb* when you plastered the well with clay or gypsum; likewise the waterskin and ships when smeared with pitch. *Al-masīʿah* is a smooth piece of wood used for plastering, which is with skilled plasterers. *Al-tasyīʿ* is plastering with it. *Al-tadhhīn* is anointing (with oil). Al-Qazzaz said: *al-siyāʿ* is plastering with lime, clay or pitch, with which ships are plastered. *Al-siyāʿ* is also the *ʿiḍāh* tree which has fruit like a pistachio, and the frankincense tree, each of which is fit to be desired. *Al-misyāʿ* is the she-camel that goes off to pasture, as if she were likened to flowing water; she is also fit for fatness, and the one that carries the family and bad care is given to her, and the one on which one travels and returns, because she is fit for people to desire her. *Asāʿahu* means he neglected him, i.e., removed what is fit for him of protection, so he became fit for destruction. (p-408) *Al-siʿwah* with kasrah means the hour, like *al-siʿwāʾ* with kasrah and ḍammah (its takhrīj has been mentioned before). It also means a foul-tongued, divorce-seeking woman, as if she were fit for swift separation like the hour. *Al-sāʿī* is the governor of any matter or people, and for the Jews and Christians it is their leader, because he is fit to strive for them and defend them. *Al-suʿāt* is management, because a person is fit for it. *Saʿyah* is a sign for a goat, because she is fit for running. *Al-suʿāwī* with ḍammah is one who endures staying awake and travel, attributed to *al-saʿy* in an eloquent way, and he is fit that one desire him. *Asʿawā bihi*, i.e., they demanded him, with the hamzah cut. *Al-sāʿah* is a part of the two new (day and night), the present time, and the Resurrection, because all of this is fit and deserving of being guarded from waste. The perishing ones are like *al-jāʿah* for the hungry, as if they wasted their hour, so they were fit for what befell them. *Sāʿah sawʿāʾ* means severe. *Sāʿat al-ibil tasūʿu* means the camels remained without a herder, so they became fit for destruction and loss. *Asāʿahu* means he neglected and wasted him, so he became so. From this is *nāqah misyāʿ*: she leaves her young until the beasts of prey eat it. *Baʿda sawʿin min al-layl wa-suwāʿ* means after a portion of the night, i.e., its calm. *Asawaʿa* means he moved from one hour to another, so he became fit to be careful, to make up in the second what he missed in the first. *Asmaʿa al-ḥimār* means the donkey released its semen, so it became fit for leaping. *Suwāʿ* is the name of an idol worshipped in the time of Noah, peace be upon him. The flood drowned it, and Iblis aroused it until it was also worshipped, because it was, in their view and their claim, fit for what they made it worthy of—exalted is God above that! *Al-wusʿ* with the three vowels means capacity and power, like *al-siʿah*; its meaning is that it is fit to bear. *Siʿahu al-shayʾ* (with kasrah) yasaʿuhu, like yaḍaʿuhu, saʿatan, like daʿatan and zinatan, means it was fit to bear it. *Allāhumma suʿ ʿalaynā* means widen (provision) for us. *Walyasaʿka baytuka* is a command to stay in it. *Hādhā al-inā' yasaʿu ʿishrīna kaylan* means this vessel holds twenty measures, i.e., it can contain them. *Al-wāsiʿ* is the opposite of narrow, like *al-waṣīʿ*. In the Most Beautiful Names: the one of abundant giving who suffices for what is asked, or the one who encompasses everything, or the one whose provision encompasses all his creation and whose mercy encompasses everything. *Al-waṣṣāʿ* like *saḥāb* is a light-spirited one in need, graceful and noble, because he is fit for what he is called to. From horses: the generous one, or the one with a wide stride. *Al-dirʿ* (the coat of mail) is like *al-waṣīʿ*. *Wasiʿa*, like *karuma*, *wisāʿah* and *siʿah* and *awsaʿa*, means he became possessed of plenty. *Allāhu ʿalayhi* means God enriched him. *Tawassaʿū fī al-majlis* means they made room, so they became fit to accommodate the one entering among them. *Wassaʿahu tawsīʿan* is the opposite of narrowing it. *Raḥmat Allāh wasiʿat kulla shayʾ* means His mercy encompassed everything. *Wasiʿa kulla shayʾ ʿilman* means He encompassed it and counted it. *Al-waʿs*, like *al-waʿd*, is a tree from which lutes and reeds are made, because it is most worthy of that among trees. Smooth sand in which walking is difficult: because it appears, due to its smoothness, fit to be walked on, but when one examines it closely, it is fit for difficulty of walking because it is sand. (p-410) *Awʿasa rakbuhu* means his riding beasts stumbled in sand. *Al-waʿsāʾ* is a soft sand hill that grows the finest herbs, because because of its softness it is the most fit of the sand hills for plants. *Makān awʿas* and *amkinah waʿs* (places that are soft sand). *Al-mīʿās* is what has turned away from roughness, so it is fit for walking in. *Al-arḍ* (the earth) that has not been trodden is fit for refraining from traveling it. *Al-ṭarīq* (the road) is fit to be traveled. Al-Qamus said: it is as if it were an opposite. *Al-muwāʿasah* is a kind of camel gait, as if it were in the middle, so it is fit for good and for racing in travel, or it is only at night. Al-Qazzaz said: a redness or yellowness appeared on his face, i.e., it was fit to appear. He said: When they mention the sandy desert (*ramalah*) they say *waʿsāʾ*, and when they mention sand (*raml*) they say *awʿas*. This is what is in the explanation of the particular lexical items on the basis of this root. As for the statements of the grammarians on the general rules of *ʿasā*, Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Qazzaz said: it is a verb that does not inflect, so you do not say *yaʿsā*, nor is it *ʿāsin*. Abd al-Haqq al-Ishbili said: no future, active participle, passive participle, or verbal noun comes from it. Al-Qazzaz said: it is accompanied by *an* (أنْ), which may be omitted, and *an* with what follows it is in the sense of a verbal noun, and it stands in the accusative position. No verbal noun or active participle follows it. This only came in the Arab proverb: *ʿasā al-Ghuwayr abʾusan* (عَسى الغُوَيْرُ أبْؤُسًا). *Abʾus* is the plural of *baʾs*, and this shows that the predicate of *ʿasā* is in the accusative position. Al-Qamus said: *al-abʾus* is calamity, and from it: *ʿasā al-Ghuwayr abʾusan*, i.e., a calamity. Abu ʿUbayd said in *Gharīb*: it is as if he meant: "perhaps al-Ghuwayr will cause misfortunes and bring misfortunes," and this is the way of the accusative. What clarifies this is the verse of al-Kumayt:

*qālū asāʾa Banū Kurzin fa-qultu lahum*
*ʿasā al-Ghuwayr bi-iʾbāsin wa-ighwārī*

The commentator Abu Muhammad ibn al-Muwaffaq, author of a commentary on the Jazuliyya, said: When ʿasā (عسى, "perhaps/it may be that") expresses hope (rajāʾ), it acquires the sense of inshāʾ (performative, non-assertive speech, such as commands, wishes and hopes), and so it is not inflected (lā yataṣarrafu). This is because inflection would contradict inshāʾ. When it is inflected, it indicates a report about the past, the present or the future, and that contradicts the meaning of inshāʾ, which does not suit the past or the future.

Some later grammarians said: ʿasā is coined for an action that is imagined to occur in the future, yet it is in the form of the past, so ʾan (أنْ) is required after it, since it has no future form.

Some others held that ʿasā is a particle (ḥarf), because it is not inflected and its meaning does not pass to other things. The correct view is that it is a verb both in form and in meaning. As for its form, this is evident, namely from the attachment of pronouns and the silent feminine tāʾ (تاءِ التَّأْنِيثِ السّاكِنَةِ). As for its meaning, it is a report of a hope (ṭamaʿ) that has occurred to the speaker. Its wording was given the form of the past because the hoping has already happened, whereas what is hoped for (al-maṭmūʿ) is that which is anticipated and awaited. ʾAn is attached to what is hoped for because it has not yet occurred. Its sisters (akhawātuhā) are stripped of ʾan because their predicate is already realised in the present, since it has begun, except for kāda (كادَ, "to be about to"), which indicates approximation in general.

Ibn Hisham al-Misri said in his Tawdīḥ: The predicate of ʿasā must be a clause (jumla). Its being a single noun is rare, as in ʿasā al-Ghuwayr ʾabʾusan (عسى الغُوَيْرُ أبْؤُسًا, "perhaps al-Ghuwayr [will bring] misfortunes"). The subject is in the nominative under ʿasā, and the verb with ʾan is in the accusative position as predicate.

Al-Radi said: It is only that ʿasā is not inflected because it includes the meaning of a particle, namely the coining of hope and expectation. His statement that ʾabʾusan and ṣāʾiman (in the example) are accusative is because ʿasā includes the meaning of kāna, so it is treated as kāna.

The view of the later grammarians is that ʿasā makes its subject nominative and its predicate accusative, like kāna.

Abu Talib al-ʿAbdi said in his commentary on al-Fārisī's Al-Īḍāḥ: Verbs are coined for inflection insofar as they are divided by the categories of time. Were it not so, verbal nouns (maṣādir) would suffice in their place. For this reason Sibawayh said: "As for verbs, they are patterns (amthila) taken from the wording of the verbal nouns of events (aḥdāth al-asmāʾ). They are built for what has passed, for what will be, and for what is existing and has not ceased." Since these verbs, meaning ʿasā, niʿma, biʾsa and the verb of wonder (fiʿl al-taʿajjub), differ from the other verbs in indication, their inflection has been abandoned permanently, because of the emphasis (mubālagha) for which they were intended in what they were made to indicate. Thus the meaning of ʿasā is hope and apprehension (ishfāq). So said Sibawayh. Since it has been restricted to this meaning, its inflection has been abandoned.

Al-Rummani said: It was prevented from inflection by analogy with laʿalla (لعلَّ, "perhaps"), just as mā was analogised to laysa (ليس). The first view is preferable, because the category of verbs should not be analogised to particles. Moreover, verbs in their own category are equivalent to particles in their category in being obligatorily indeclinable (luzūm al-bināʾ). Rather, nouns are analogised to verbs, as you say of qaṭām and ḥazām (names of ʾamr-like words) that they are indeclinable because they occupy the position of a verb, and that interrogative nouns are indeclinable because they occupy the position of a particle. You do not say of verbs that they are indeclinable by analogy with particles, nor that particles are indeclinable by analogy with verbs. Rather, each of them is a root, and likewise its inflection. Its refusal to inflect is not because it is analogised to a particle and runs its course. ʿAsā is among the sisters of kāna, but it was not mentioned with them because of its difference: it lacks inflection, its predicate requires ʾan, and it is a verb.

What indicates that it is among the sisters of kāna is ʿasā al-Ghuwayr ʾabʾusan, since the root has been uncovered, as the root of aqāma (أقامَ, "to establish") and aṭāla (أطالَ, "to prolong") and the like has been uncovered, by the poet's words:

You turned away and prolonged the aversion, and union rarely endures under prolonged aversion.

The verb's obligatory connection with its predicate is because it is made a substitute for the inflection that ought to belong to it. As for the obligatory presence of ʾan, it is because the sentence is directed toward an interpretation of the future, and ʾan reaches that meaning. The line cited as an example contains something curious: it is a plural verbal noun (maṣdar majmūʿ) occupying the position of a verbal noun which occupies the position of a verb. Verbal nouns in their basic form are not pluralised, but this is a necessity of poetry and a proverbial usage. The root is that baʾs (بَأْسٌ, "misfortune") becomes ʾabʾus (أبْؤُسٌ). This ends the words of al-ʿAbdi.

In my view, when the meaning for which it is used, namely hope or apprehension, is strengthened, its predicate is made a noun, as a warning that it is now like kāna, because of the strong resemblance between them. Abu Talib said: When ʾan and the verb follow it, the clause is in the nominative position, and the length of the sentence takes the place of the predicate. Its meaning, which is apprehension and hope, is close to the approximation of kāda. Therefore ʾan is omitted from its predicate, treating it as kāda, just as they permitted ʾan to enter the predicate of kāda, treating it as ʿasā.

The commentator on the Jazuliyya said: Omitting ʾan from the predicate of ʿasā is more common than attaching ʾan to the predicate of kāda, because kāda approximates the act itself, and ʾan contradicts that. He said: Among the differences between them is that ʿasā does not take a pronoun of the matter or story (ḍamīr al-shaʾn wa al-qiṣṣa), because of its resemblance to a particle, since it is not inflected, whereas kāda does take it, because it is inflected. Then he preferred the view that it does take it, even though it is not inflected, just as it is taken in niʿma and biʾsa.

Ibn Hisham al-Khadrawi also said in his commentary on al-Īḍāḥ: Sibawayh estimated ʿasā as qāraba (قارَبَ, "to come near"), meaning that it makes its subject nominative and its object accusative, because qāraba is transitive. He estimated it as qaruba (قَرُبَ, "to be near"), meaning that it does not put the object in the accusative, because that verb is not transitive. He said: ʿAsā does not enter upon the past. Abu ʿAli said: This is because it indicates pure future, and for this reason ʾan follows it, so it is not suitable for the past in any way.

The commentator on the Jazuliyya said: ʿAsā with an apparent noun has two views. One is that it is defective (nāqiṣa) in the sense of defective kāna, requiring a subject and a predicate, except that its predicate must be a verb. It originally should be a noun like the predicate of kāna, but it was diverted to the verb to indicate clearly what is intended by hope and to strengthen what hope conveys of futurity. It is compared in this respect to qāraba Zaydun al-khurūja (قارَبَ زَيْدٌ الخُرُوجَ, "Zayd came close to going out"), for the sake of clarifying the grammatical analysis, not in meaning, since qāraba Zaydun al-khurūja contains no coining of hope or anything else. It is merely an illustration of the estimated verbal inflection, since that is its original form. The coining of hope came upon it later, as it did with the verb of wonder, niʿma, biʾsa and others.

The second view is that it comes as a complete verb (tāmma), used like qaruba, so it takes ʾan with the verb: ʿasā ʾan yaqūma Zaydun (عسى أنْ يَقُومَ زَيْدٌ, "Zayd may stand"). It dispenses, with ʾan and the verb, with both predicates, as ẓanantu ʾan yaqūma Zaydun (ظَنَنْتُ أنْ يَقُومَ زَيْدٌ) dispenses with the two objects. This is because it contains a predicate and a subject, which is the purpose of these verbs. When you say Zaydun ʿasā ʾan yaqūma, it may be that ʿasā is defective, in which case there is a pronoun referring to Zayd as its subject, and ʾan with the verb is its predicate. It may also be complete, in which case there is no pronoun in it, and ʾan with the verb is its subject.

Ibn al-Khabbaz al-Mawsili said in his book al-Nihāya fī Sharḥ Kifāyat al-Kifāya: ʿAsā is for hope, for the emphasis of hope, so its predicate cannot be past, because its meaning is hope and expectation, and the past is not hoped for or expected, since it has already happened. He argued that it is used only for the future with the verse of one of the poets of al-Ḥamāsa:

Perhaps the Tayyi' from among the Tayyi', after this, will extinguish the burning griefs of the liver and the ribs.

He brought in sīn (س) because it was not possible to bring in ʾan in the verse. The commentator on the Jazuliyya said, in substance: It obligatorily took the verb as its predicate to indicate the future, and it obligatorily took ʾan to strengthen that. For this reason its predicate is not a noun, although its original form is a noun, since a noun does not indicate time. And sīn and sawfa could not be put in its place, because they indicate a deferment in time. The purpose here is to bring it closer. It occurs rarely in poetry. He recited the verse mentioned above.

Ibn al-Khabbaz said: The entry of the interrogative upon it indicates that it is not for hope, because the interrogative does not enter upon hope or upon what is not a report. Thus the entry of hal (هَلْ) upon it indicates that it is a report. End quote.

So the interpretation I have mentioned, that it is for what may possibly be and is apt to be, is the first; and the hope is a necessary implication of the sentence's content, not what it denotes by direct signification (muṭābaqa). And God is the Granter of success.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 9, verse 19:

When Allah, glorified is He, had made clear the one who is righteous for this matter, distinct from others, He denounced those who did not distinguish between the two categories, and said: ﴿Do you consider the providing of water for the pilgrims﴾, meaning: stripped of faith, ﴿and the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque﴾, meaning: likewise, like faith in Allah, the Last Day and jihad. The people of the provision of water and the maintenance (of the Mosque), without faith, in their allegiance (to one another) and in refraining from hostility towards them, ﴿are like one who believes in Allah﴾, meaning: the one whom the belief in His perfection drives toward every perfection, ﴿and the Last Day﴾, meaning: the one whose fear of it urges him to every good, ﴿and strives in the way of Allah﴾, meaning: the King, the Most High, who encompasses everything. So the verse, according to the reading of the majority, is an instance of ihtibak (elision): he omitted first the comparandum (al-mushabbah) because the comparatum (al-mushabbah bihi) indicates it, and second the comparatum because the comparandum indicates it. As for the anomalous reading of Nasiy ibn Wardan from Abu Ja'far, "suqat wa 'amarat" (in the plural), no estimation (of an omitted element) is needed.

When it was as if it were said: "We used to think that; so what is their state?", He said: ﴿They are not equal in the sight of Allah﴾, meaning: the One to whom all perfection belongs, because the polytheists did wrong by abandoning faith. ﴿And Allah﴾, meaning: the One to whom all command belongs, and there is no command for anyone along with Him, ﴿does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ (p-417) meaning: those who put things in other than their proper places. Disbelief is the greatest wrong. So do not make guidance obligatory for them, nor equality with the guided, even if they engage in all the actions of the guided apart from faith. Whoever among you does that is a wrongdoer, and there is fear for him of losing that which necessitates guidance.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 9, verse 20:

When he negated equality for them without explicitly naming those who are preferred (al-tarjih), so that the longing for the explicit statement would intensify, and it would thereby be more firmly fixed in the soul and more weighty in the heart, it was as if it were said: "Who, then, is the preferred?" So he said: ﴿Those who believed﴾, meaning: they performed this act, which is the belief of the one addressed, so that they do not deny him in anything of what he reports from Allah. He restricted the verb (qasr, restriction), though it is originally transitive (muta'addin), to indicate that there is no belief other than this; and if something else is found, it is considered non-existent in relation to it. Likewise, every verb that is restricted follows this pattern, to indicate that because of its great benefit, there is no other act of its kind. ﴿And emigrated and struggled﴾.

Since the one spoken of earlier was the one who struggles in the way of Allah, the context required placing it (the struggle) before the instrument (al-alah). This differs from what occurs at the end of al-Anfal, for the context there required placing wealth and self first, because of what was previously stated of its requirement in more than one verse, as its explanation has passed. Also, at this time wealth had become abundant, while the places of jihad had become distant, so attention to the path (al-sabil) was fitting. Therefore he placed ﴿in the way of Allah﴾ first, meaning: sincerely for Him, because He is the King for whom there is no equal. Then he followed it with His saying: ﴿with their wealth and their selves﴾, explicitly mentioning the self to encourage direct engagement with it. ﴿They are greater in rank﴾, meaning: in terms of elevation of rank (al-daraja), which is the excellence that brings one close to Allah.

Since the only consideration is what is with Him, glory be to Him, and not what is with people, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿with Allah﴾, meaning: with the Greatest King, from among the people of the watering of the pilgrims and what accompanies it, without belief indicated by its evidences. He did not mention the one they are preferred over, in order to indicate that their excellence is absolute, so the one they are preferred over is included in what is indicated. He repeated the greatest Name for the sake of added encouragement, because of the gravity of the situation and the difficulty of the aim. This also conveys that those acts are noble in themselves, so whoever engages in them is on a great rank compared to whoever does not engage in them, and whoever builds them upon the foundation (of faith) is greater still. Then he clarified what pertains to the people of his party, saying: ﴿And those are﴾, meaning: those elevated in soil (al-'alu al-turba), ﴿they﴾, meaning: exclusively, not you, O boasters, with polytheism, ﴿the successful﴾, meaning: attaining the lasting good in both abodes, to the exclusion of all others, even if they perform whatever good deeds they perform. This is because they have ascended from servanthood ('abdiyya) to nearness to Him ('indiyya).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 9, verse 21:

Having explained that the recompense of those (who do not believe) is eternal abiding in the Fire, he now explained what is for these (believers), saying, explaining their triumph: ﴿Their Lord gives them good news﴾, that is, the One who does good to them by guiding them and choosing them. Consider this good news, which indicates the loftiness of their station, since it comes without any intermediary. And that the good news matches the one who gives it indicates that this good news is a great good news, having no end and whose magnitude cannot be fully grasped. ﴿Of mercy﴾, that is, great mercy, and He increased its greatness (p-419) by His saying: ﴿from Him﴾, and this is an indication that there is no salvation without pardon. Then He informed that mercy, just as it produced pardon, which is the lowest of the stations, brought them happiness with its highest, so He said: ﴿and good pleasure﴾, that is, that they be pleased with God for being content with God's decree. This occurs when one restricts his gaze to God, for he never changes at all because of any of His decrees, just as God, who is his Merciful One, does not change. Whoever's gaze is directed to seeking a share for himself is always in a state of change, from joy to sorrow, from happiness to grief, from comfort to pain, and from pleasure to suffering. Thus it is established that complete mercy is attained only by one who is content with God's decree, and God is pleased with him, so that his soul is content and pleasing. For this reason He did not restrict it with "from Him." And these two (mercy and good pleasure) are in this world and the Hereafter.

When He mentioned this spiritual garden bestowed upon them in this world, He followed it with the explanation of the spiritual and physical garden specific to the abode in which they will remain. So He said: ﴿And gardens﴾, that is, orchards abundant in trees and fruits, ﴿for them therein is lasting bliss﴾, that is, very great bliss, pure from any kind of turbidity. And He indicated eternity by His saying: ﴿enduring﴾.

Then he explicitly stated their eternal abiding therein by using the word "khulud" (abiding), so that it would be more soothing to the soul, saying: ﴿abiding therein﴾. He confirmed the matter with his words: ﴿forever﴾. Then he resumed the praise, signaling more to come, with his words: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, i.e., the One to whom belongs absolute self-sufficiency (al-ghina al-mutlaq) and complete power, ﴿with Him is a great reward﴾. And how much is conveyed by the description "great" applied to the Great One! He singled out these believers for this reward, whose permanence was expressed by these three phrases linked with glorification and the Greatest Name, so it was the greatest of rewards, because (p-420) their faith is the greatest of faiths.

When he had finished with attachment (*al-'atifa*) to the excellence of deeds, he turned to attachment through lineage and wealth. He placed the first before the second to indicate that kinship in conduct takes precedence over all other circumstances. Since the object of *al-muwalat* (loyal allegiance) is *al-munasara* (support), and support from fathers and brothers is greater than support from others, because its source is the abundance of helpers and intimate companions, he restricted the address to them and said: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, meaning: those who have affirmed with their tongues their belief in their Lord, turning away from whatever else is set up as a rival, visible or otherwise. Confirm your claim to that by ﴿not taking﴾, meaning: not deliberately or artificially setting out to take, ﴿your fathers and your brothers as allies﴾, meaning: in accordance with what natural inclinations call for and what the strengthening of desires encourages, so that you would confide your secrets to them and prefer their pleasure and their standing with them. ﴿If they prefer﴾, meaning: seek and bring about the preference, ﴿disbelief﴾, which is the concealment of the truth and the denial of it, ﴿over faith﴾. By the form *istaf'ala* (the form expressing seeking or pursuing) he indicates that faith, because of the abundance of its excellences and the clarity of its evidences, is naturally beloved, so no one abandons it except through a kind of forcing and arrogance against his intellect and a struggle.

Since the most precious thing is the religion, and it cannot be attained except through guidance, and since it has already been stated that guidance is withdrawn from the wrongdoer, and since he warned them against its being taken away by saying: ﴿And whoever among you allies with them﴾, meaning: deliberately undertakes to treat them in their affairs as a close relative treats his close relative, ﴿then those﴾, meaning: those who are removed from the divine presences, ﴿are the wrongdoers﴾, meaning: because they have placed allegiance where it does not belong, (p-421) after He, glory be to Him, had previously addressed them with such admonitions. This is a return, by way of caution, to ﴿And those of blood relationship are more entitled to one another﴾ [al-Anfal: 75], to the end of the verse, concerning the *wilaya* (guardianship and allegiance) that clarifies the true believers, and an indication that He leads them astray and does not guide them, in accordance with the earlier report that He does not guide the wrongdoing people.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 9, verse 24:

Since souls differ in their aspirations and vary in their natures and dispositions, this was not sufficient as a warning to all of them. So he followed it with a warning more severe than it, directed at those souls. He said, shifting from the mode of approach to the station of aversion, which signals the rebukes of anger: ﴿Say﴾, that is: O greatest of creation in compassion, gentleness and sincere counsel, to those who are not led by what has preceded of rebukes to believe that they must bear all these harms in this world so that the religion remains intact and is not breached: ﴿If your fathers﴾, that is, those whom you hold in the greatest reverence, ﴿and your sons﴾, that is, those who are the dearest people to you and the most beloved to you, ﴿and your brothers﴾, that is, those who are of your own origin, so they are like your own selves, ﴿and your spouses﴾, that is, those who are a dwelling for you, ﴿and your kinsfolk﴾, that is, those through whom comes complete comfort and the upholding of honour and protection, and they are the nearest people of a man, those who associate with him.

When He, glory be to Him, had mentioned what takes precedence over wealth in the eyes of the people of lofty aspirations, He said: ﴿and wealth you have acquired﴾, that is, which you have gained through effort, including travel and other means, for your livelihood; ﴿and commerce whose slackness you fear﴾, that is, for fear of missing the times of its brisk demand because of your preoccupation with what God, glory be to Him, has urged, so that it causes to be lost, as you imagine, that by which your sustenance is maintained; ﴿and dwellings with which you are pleased﴾, that is, because they gather all of that. He, glory be to Him, arranged them in the best order: the father is the most beloved of those mentioned here because of the element of support in him, then the son, then the brother, then the spouse, then the kinsfolk who comprise both males and females, then wealth in hand, then the profit expected from trade. He concluded with the dwelling because it is the ultimate end, of which all that preceded are means to find rest and adornment within it. ﴿More beloved to you than God﴾, that is, the One who combines the attributes of perfection, who has bestowed upon you all that has been mentioned, and who, whenever He wills, can strip them from you; ﴿and His Messenger﴾, that is, the one who brought you what preserves these blessings in both abodes; ﴿and striving in His way﴾, that is, to return the strayed of His servants to Him and to gather them upon Him. In His saying ﴿then wait﴾, that is, await while waiting, is an eloquent threat; ﴿until God brings His command﴾, that is, the One who has encompassing knowledge of everything; ﴿His command﴾, that is, the One whose reality your attributes cannot reach and your strength cannot bear.

Since whoever prefers the love of any of those things over His love, the Exalted, has departed from His religion and turned back to the religion of whoever he preferred, the sense is: then He will strike you with a calamity you cannot endure and by which you will not be guided to avert it through any kind of remedy, because you have chosen for yourselves opposition to guidance. It is known that whoever is like this is stamped with corruption, so He linked to it His saying: ﴿And God﴾, that is, the One who combines the attributes of perfection, ﴿does not guide the people﴾, that is, He does not create guidance in the hearts of ﴿the defiant ones﴾, that is, those who employed the power of standing that they possess in pursuing corruption they desire, until defiance, which is going out of what ought to remain and be bound to, and which here is obedience, becomes a trait of their character and an inseparable attribute of them. Rather, He leaves them to their own souls, so they lose both this world and the Hereafter.

When some souls were, by the pride in their numbers, in a state of intoxication that made them heedless of some of the places where Allah's power operates, He related the story of Hunayn as evidence for what He had left vague of the threat. This answers a questioner who seemed to ask: "What is that matter which is awaited and feared because of its great importance?" So it was said: "Humiliation, disgrace, neediness and brokenness." It was then as if it were said: "And how will that happen?" So it was said: by the Almighty empowering over you, though you are many, strong people other than you, though they are few and weak, just as He empowered you, when you were like that, until you came to the state you are in. ﴿Allah had already given you victory﴾, that is, the Supreme King, despite your extreme weakness, ﴿on many occasions﴾, that is, in stations, positions and places where you settled yourselves to meet your enemy, ﴿many﴾, that is, of the raids that came before you, such as Badr, Qurayza, al-Nadir, Qaynuqa', al-Hudaybiyya, Khaybar and other contests with the disbelievers. You were in a condition of humiliation, scarcity and brokenness in which your victory and superiority over all the disbelievers could not be imagined, while you were among them like a white hair on the hide of a black bull. He did not leave you to the support of those whose affair had been settled for you by boycotting them. This shows that whoever obeys Allah and prefers religion over worldly life, Allah gives him both religion and worldly life in the best manner, even if all people oppose him. And what follows concerning the story of Hunayn shows that whoever relies on worldly life loses both religion and worldly life, unless Allah overtakes him with a mercy from Him and he returns with it. Then the Exalted said: ﴿And on the day﴾, that is, and He gave you victory after He had strengthened and multiplied you, He alone, not your multitude and strength, on the day of ﴿Hunayn﴾, which is a valley between Makkah and al-Ta'if, beside Dhu al-Majaz, closer to Makkah, beyond 'Arafat to the north.

Since Salama ibn Salama ibn Waqsh al-Ansari (may Allah be pleased with him) had said, when the two hosts met and the multitude of people impressed him: "We will not be defeated today through lack of numbers!", the Prophet (ﷺ) was displeased with his words, and he should rely on none but Allah. Admiration was a deadly poison to the means (of victory). Allah the Glorified taught us in this battle by mentioning the evil effect of it, so that we might beware of it. Then the Glorified returned to bestowing favor, because the one who said it was a single person whose statement others disliked. He said: ﴿When﴾, that is, when ﴿your multitude impressed you﴾, that is, so you concluded from it that no conqueror could overcome it. The Glorified attributed the verb to the group, as an indication that because of their high station it should not be that any of them would say such a thing. ﴿But it did not avail you anything﴾, that is, it did not suffice you in any way. ﴿And the earth became constricted for you﴾, that is, the wide earth ﴿despite its vastness﴾, that is, despite its breadth, so that you did not see any place in it that would shelter you from what you were in, because of the extreme terror. In reality, nothing was constricted except the hopes that had come to rest in wealth and men. Perhaps its conjunction, by the particle of delay in His saying ﴿then you turned back﴾, that is, you turned your backs to the disbelievers in great numbers, and He confirmed that with His saying ﴿fleeing﴾, that is, in rout, although the flight occurred at the moment of encounter and was not delayed, is an indication of the enslavement they had felt, through reliance on strength and numbers.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 9, verse 26:

﴿Then Allah sent down﴾, meaning He who encompasses all the attributes of perfection, ﴿His tranquility (sakinah)﴾, meaning His mercy. It is the matter that calms hearts so that they are not moved by the trials that befall them, through trust in Him, glorified is He, witnessing His most holy presence, and being free of need for anything else.

Since the context concerns the Messenger, and since supporting the one who claims prophethood is among the signs of his truthfulness in claiming that he is a messenger and that the One who sent him is able to do what He wills, especially if that support comes in a manner that breaks custom, He expressed it this way rather than by describing him as a prophet. So He said: ﴿upon His Messenger﴾, meaning in addition to the tranquility he already had, a tranquility that no one else was granted in its like. By it, thirty thousand, twenty thousand, or four thousand were kept firm, according to the differing reports, and in ten persons, or a hundred, or three hundred, also according to the differing reports. Their steadfastness was not possible except through it. Then that did not increase him except in advancing, to the point that al-'Abbas, his paternal uncle, and Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith, his cousin, may Allah be pleased with them both, were holding back his mule from advancing too far. Perhaps the use of ﴿thumma﴾ (then) for the conjunction indicates the high rank of that steadfastness and the improbability that its like should occur within the ordinary course of things. ﴿And upon the believers﴾, meaning as for those among them who were steadfast, it was in addition to what they already had of that; and as for others, they were given what (p-٤٢٦) they did not have at that time. This is because when the people had fled, the Prophet (ﷺ) said to his uncle al-'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "Call out to them, O 'Abbas!" So he called out, and he had a loud voice: "O servants of Allah! O companions of the tree! O companions of Surat al-Baqarah!" Then they turned back as one body, saying: "At your service, at your service!" It is also possible that the mention of the Messenger, peace be upon him, is merely for the sake of blessing, as in the mention of Allah in His saying: ﴿So that for Allah is one-fifth of it﴾ [al-Anfal: 41], and as an increase in magnifying the favor bestowed by it, because souls are more inclined to what the Messenger gives from it, and hearts are more receptive to it, out of belief in his majesty, greatness, and perfection. ﴿And He sent down﴾, meaning from the heaven, ﴿hosts you did not see﴾, meaning of the angels, upon them be peace. ﴿And He punished﴾, meaning by killing, capture, defeat, taking captives, and plunder, ﴿those who disbelieved﴾. He expressed it with the verb because among them were some who believed after that.

Since the punishment inflicted upon those who brought about this very description was great, He followed it with a statement of the recompense of those deeply entrenched in it, as a warning to whoever prefers love of something of what has passed over love of Allah. So He said: ﴿And that﴾, meaning the punishment of which what was inflicted upon these people is a part, and other than it, ﴿is the recompense of the disbelievers﴾, meaning those firmly established in the attribute of disbelief, who preferred love of those who preceded them, of the fathers and others, over Allah, and so they persisted in following their fathers in falsehood after they had seen proofs that outshine the sun and leave no room for doubt. As for those whose disbelief was not firmly established, that was a good outcome for them, because it led them to Islam. Thus it is clear that the one who is victorious is the one whom Allah helps, whether few or many, and that fewness, multitude, strength, and weakness are equal in relation to His power. So do not be deceived by the blessings He has bestowed upon you, for He is able to strip them away, and no one deserves anything from Him, and no one can avert His decree. In this is an indication that no one turns back after his faith except one who was deeply entrenched in disbelief, and in it is the most eloquent warning: for if He punishes those who merely brought disbelief into being for a time, how much more those who became deeply rooted in it!

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 9, verse 27:

When he had explained that the punishment is the recompense of the disbelievers, he explained that He turns in repentance to whomever of them He wills, namely everyone in whom He knows a capacity for faith, even if he was severe in the attribute of disbelief. So He said, coordinating with ﴿And He punished﴾ [al-Tawbah: 26]: ﴿Then Allah turns in forgiveness﴾, that is, He Who has encompassing knowledge and power. And since no one's repentance would fill the period of distance, He introduced the preposition and said: ﴿after that﴾, that is, after the great punishment, ﴿to whom He wills﴾, that is, He guides him to Islam and forgives him all the sins that preceded. ﴿And Allah﴾, that is, the One Who possesses the attributes of perfection, ﴿is Forgiving, Merciful﴾, that is, the Eraser of sins, of great honor toward whoever repents. In this there is an indication that He made this event, for His wisdom which required linking effects to their causes, a cause for the Islam of those among the Quraysh disbelievers and others who attended it, the muallafah (those whose hearts were won over), by what He distributed among them, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, of the booty of Hawazin, and by what they saw of the might and exaltation of Islam. There was in this an encouragement for them through wealth and an intimidation through the assaults of battle. And for the Islam of the delegation of Hawazin, because of what befell them of subjugation and what they witnessed of the great victory of the Prophet (ﷺ). And for the Islam of others among the Arabs, because each of them knew of this event that they (the Muslims' enemies) were weakest in support and fewest in number. All of this was mercy from Him, glorified is He, toward them and gentleness toward them. All of it occurred as He indicated: the Tulaqa' embraced Islam and their Islam was good, and the delegation of Hawazin came and asked the Prophet (ﷺ) to restore to them what had been taken from them. He said to them: "I delayed [the distribution] for your sake, but when you were slow, I divided their spoils among the people. So choose: the wealth or the captives!" They chose the captives, and he interceded for them with the people, and they responded to him, so he returned to them their sons and women, out of mercy from him toward them. The Arabs were humbled by that and entered the religion in multitudes. He concluded this verse with forgiveness and mercy, as is most fitting to the context of repentance. That he did not turn to concluding the first verse with ﴿Knowing, Wise﴾ [al-Tawbah: 15] except because of what he established, making the ام in ﴿Or did you think﴾ [al-Tawbah: 16] equivalent to the hamzah. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 9, verse 28:

When the discussion of the commands and prohibitions, and the clarification of the wisdoms that encourage and deter, had gone so far that it left no room for anyone who holds even the slightest attachment to the religion to pay attention to the corrupters, He explained that the reason for repelling them and for severing ties with them firmly is that they are impure (najas), and that the places in which the lights of His greatness and majesty appeared, upon which the suns of His prophethood and message shone, in which the lightning of His might flashed, and in which the swords of His prohibition and command moved about, are places of holiness and abodes of intimacy. Whoever approaches them without being of their people is burned by their fire, and the brilliance of their lights dazzles his sight. Thus, drawing a conclusion and deducing from what preceded, He said: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, meaning: those who have affirmed faith with their tongues and who are among those who find lying repugnant. ﴿Indeed, the polytheists﴾, meaning: those who are deeply immersed in polytheism, as evidenced by their persistence in it.

Since they were characterized by it, and since they did not wash themselves or their garments of impurity, the description of them with impurity was intensified by making them the very essence of it, so He said: ﴿impure (najas)﴾, meaning: while you claim that you are the furthest of people from impurity, both physically and spiritually. Therefore they must be loathed, kept away, and avoided, as is done with an impure thing, because of the evil traits they embody and the bad characteristics they possess. As for their bodies, the jurists agree that they are pure, because the Prophet (ﷺ) drank from their vessels and did not forbid eating with them, nor did he order washing from them; had they been impure, Islam would not have purified them. Since their being kept away followed from this, He said: ﴿So let them not approach﴾, meaning: the polytheists. This is a prohibition addressed to the Muslims against allowing them such access, and it was expressed as a prohibition upon them for the sake of emphasis. ﴿the Sacred Mosque﴾, meaning: the one from which they expelled you while you were the purest of people. He made the time general, dropping the preposition, and alerted them to the goodness of the time and the abundance of good in it by expressing it with the general term, so He said: ﴿after this year of theirs﴾. He established the matter and removed ambiguity with His words: ﴿this﴾, which is the last year of the ninth year, the year of the delegations, the year of his (ﷺ) return from the expedition of Tabuk. He expressed it by their approaching rather than their coming, after having given the prior warning that no polytheist would be accepted except Islam or death, indicating the expulsion of the polytheists from the Arabian Peninsula, and that no two religions may gather in it, because it is entirely the locus of Arab prophethood and the place of divine secrets. Whoever is in it, even at its farthest end, has come close to all that is in it, and in relation to the Sacred Precinct it is then like the courtyards of houses and the open spaces of mosques. In the Sahih, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Prophet (ﷺ) sent Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) as commander of the Hajj after his return from Tabuk, then sent after him ʿAli (may Allah be pleased with him), and commanded him to proclaim the Bara'ah. Abu Hurayrah said: ʿAli proclaimed with us on the day of sacrifice among the people of Mina the Bara'ah, and that no polytheist should perform Hajj after this year, and that no one naked should circumambulate the House. This is an ancient practice; Allah the Exalted commanded the Children of Israel in more than one place in the Torah that they should not leave any polytheist in all the lands of the Holy House (Bayt al-Maqdis), in contrast to other lands which Allah would grant them. Among what the translator stated at the end of the Fifth Book is: "When you advance toward a village or a city to fight its people, call them to peace. If they accept and open to you, all who are in it of men shall become servants to you and pay you tribute. But if they do not accept peace and wage war against you, then fight them and besiege them; for the LORD your God will deliver it into your hand, and you will strike down everyone in it with the sword. Thus you shall do to all the distant cities which are not cities of these peoples. But in the cities of these peoples which the LORD your God is giving you as an inheritance, you shall not leave alive anything that breathes, but you shall utterly destroy them, so that they may not teach you to do according to all their abominations which they have done for their gods." Similar things are many in it, and what came after it in the Torah is what I have mentioned. And Allah is the Granter of success.

The totality of the lands of Islam with respect to the disbelievers is of three categories. The first is the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), where it is not permitted for a disbeliever to enter under any circumstances, based on the apparent meaning of this verse. The second is the Hijaz and what is under its ruling, which is the Arabian Peninsula; a disbeliever may enter it with permission, but may not remain longer than the duration of a journey, three days, because the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Expel the polytheists from the Arabian Peninsula." It extends from the farthest point of ʿAden Abyan in the south to the edges of Syria in the north in length, and from Jeddah, which is the westernmost extremity of the Peninsula on the shore of the Indian Ocean, to the countryside of Iraq in the east in breadth. The third is the rest of the lands of Islam, in which it is permitted for a disbeliever to reside under protection and safe conduct for as long as he wishes, but he may not enter the mosques except with the permission of a Muslim. This is what al-Baghawi mentioned. Ibn al-Furat said in his history, at the account of Bukhtanassar's invasion of the Children of Israel and of the land of the Arabs: "The lands of the Arabs were only called a peninsula (jazirah) because the seas and rivers surround them, so they became like a peninsula among the peninsulas of the sea. This is because the Euphrates came from the lands of the Romans and appeared from the direction of Qinnasrin, then descended upon the Jazirah and the black land of Iraq until it fell into the sea from the direction of Basra and al-Ubullah, and the sea extended from that place encircling the lands of the Arabs. From it a branch reached Kazimah and extended to al-Qatif, Hajar, Oman, and al-Shajar, and a branch inclined from it toward Hadramawt, the region of Abhar, and Aden. That branch lengthened and pierced into the Tihamah of Yemen and proceeded to the coast of Jeddah. The Nile came from the upper lands of the Sudan on the western side of this branch, extending parallel to the sea with it, until it fell into the sea of Egypt and Syria.
