Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 9, verse 126:

Since the implied meaning, as a consequence of the ruling he had affirmed about their deep-rootedness in impurity (rijs) and their increase in it, is: "Do they not see their persistence in hypocrisy and their steadfastness in it?", he followed it with a reminder to them of the punishment of this world and a rebuke to them in His saying: ﴿Do they not see?﴾, i.e., the hypocrites. Al-Rummani said: "The seeing here is of the heart, because sight of the eye does not govern a clause, since a thing is not seen from different aspects." ﴿That they﴾, i.e., the hypocrites. Since the mere occurrence of trial is a form of punishment, he used the passive form in His saying: ﴿are tested﴾, i.e., they are mixed up with the events of time and the calamities of circumstances, with what compels them to reveal their characters by displaying what lies hidden of their hypocrisy. ﴿Every year﴾, i.e., even when people are at their most fertile and their lives most elevated, ﴿once or twice﴾, so they are exposed by that. This necessitates repentance, because whoever knows their hidden secrets, which they strive to conceal, knows everything and is capable of everything, and so He is worthy that His commands be obeyed and His warnings feared.

Since their not repenting despite being tested in this manner is improbable, he indicated it with the particle of delay, saying: ﴿Then they do not repent﴾, i.e., they do not renew repentance, ﴿nor do they﴾, i.e., with their hearts, ﴿remember﴾, i.e., even the slightest remembrance, as indicated by the idgham (the assimilation of the letters in the verb). Had it not been that they gained an increase in impurity, the repeated trial would have been likely to weaken their impurity until it removed it. But whenever it weakens one thing, it is followed by its like or something greater, because of the increases that result from the presence of the Qur'an's installments. Remembrance is the seeking of recollection of the meaning of disbelief in it. So the verse censures them for not repenting, despite being struck by calamities, because they do not remember (p-54) that He, glorified is He, has struck them with these only because of their sins. ﴿And He pardons much﴾ [al-Shura: 30]. Just as one of them does not punish his servant except for a sin, and as long as he does not repent, he continues to punish him.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 9, verse 127:**

When he mentioned what they say of mockery, he followed it up, as emphasis for the increase in their disbelief and as clarification of his depiction of what arises from their act of mockery of faith and of winking at one another with their eyes, saying: ﴿And when﴾, and he emphasized with the negative particle, saying: "mā" (not). Since the purpose was the very act of sending down and not the specifying of what was sent down, he put into the passive form his words: ﴿a surah is sent down﴾, meaning a portion of the Qur'an, ﴿some of them look at others﴾, meaning the hypocrites, ﴿at one another﴾, meaning winking in derision and mockery, saying: ﴿"Does anyone see you?"﴾ And they emphasized the generality, so they said: ﴿"from anyone"﴾, meaning from the believers, if you leave. So if hearing the like of this is grievous to us [and it is grievous to us], and it is grievous to us that the believers should become aware of this secret of ours.

Since their leaving such a situation was abominable, he indicated the severity of its ugliness with the particle of delay, saying: ﴿then they turn away﴾, meaning: even if no one sees them; and if one of the believers sees them, they endure the hardship and remain steadfast. Since they deserved every evil, he told of them in the form of supplication, with his words: ﴿Allah has turned away﴾, meaning He who possesses absolute self-sufficiency and all perfection, ﴿their hearts﴾, meaning from faith. Then he gave the reason for that with his words: ﴿because they are a people﴾, who, although they have power over what they attempt, ﴿do not understand﴾, meaning their hearts are naturally disposed to not comprehending, because of the coarseness that is in them. (p-55) This is an indication of the ending of the verse before it. These two verses, which end with ﴿do not understand﴾, follow the command to fight in his words: ﴿Fight those of the disbelievers who are near you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 123], which corresponds to ﴿Go forth, light and heavy﴾ [al-Tawbah: 41], the verse. They contain, together with their brevity, the essence of the attributes of the hypocrites that follow the verse ﴿Go forth﴾ [al-Tawbah: 41], which concludes with the general of them regarding the people of the settled areas in his words: ﴿Those of wealth among them ask your permission﴾ [al-Tawbah: 86], with ﴿they understand﴾ [al-Tawbah: 87], then upon repeating their mention with ﴿they do not know﴾ [al-Tawbah: 93]. Directing these two verses to the people of the settled areas is evident, since they are among those who frequently attend the descent of the Reminder, while both verses remain open to generality. The ending here with ﴿do not understand﴾ is more fitting, because the context, which is the consideration of the increase of faith in relation to them, requires reflection and contemplation, although with regard to the believers it is in the utmost clarity.

[p. 56] When the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to convey these very difficult matters in this surah, and it was known that no one bears them except one whom Allah the Exalted has enabled, while the hypocrites dislike them and their turning away indicated their aversion, He made them aware that the matter called for their motives to be drawn to loving this caller (dā'ī) to them, which requires them to remain with him and to keep far from what they do to him by turning away from him. [He made them aware] that his states calling them to love him are greater than the states of their fathers, which obligated them to have love for him and obligations toward him, which they boast of being involved in and of exceeding in. And [He made them aware] that all the honor and nobility in this world that is gained through this Qur'an belongs to everyone who believes in it. So He said: ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger﴾.

Since the Messenger must be honored and served for the sake of the One who sent him, even if stripped of every other attribute, He began to mention to them some of his attributes that call for greater honor toward him. He said: ﴿from among yourselves﴾, meaning: you return with him to a single origin, in that you share a close father, and that is closer to familiarity and quicker to understanding the proof, and further from stubbornness and obstinacy. ﴿Grievous to him is what distresses you﴾, meaning: he is extremely difficult for him. The word ʿizzah (grievousness) means the refusal of a thing in a way that makes whatever one seeks from it impossible, whether through power, scarcity, or difficulty. And ʿanat means the affliction that befalls a person, which constricts the chest and for which one finds no way out. ﴿Ardently desirous (ḥarīṣ)﴾, meaning: intensely eager ﴿over you﴾, meaning: for your benefit. And ḥirṣ (eagerness) means the intense seeking of a thing with striving in it. He placed the prepositional phrase first to indicate restriction, and said: ﴿for the believers﴾, meaning: those who are of this description, all of them, especially. When He mentioned the attribute that calls for firmness, He placed first what calls for compassion toward one who has a connection to him through what calls for kinship. So He said: ﴿Kind (raʾūf)﴾, meaning: extremely merciful to whoever has from him affection and connection, in accordance with the meaning of raʾfah (tenderness) mentioned shortly before.

Since the believer is figuratively applied to one who is capable of faith, and his connection now is not actual but potential, He said, generalizing his mercy (ﷺ) as is fitting for the nobility of his station and the greatness of his character: ﴿Merciful (raḥīm)﴾. For these kinds of intentions of the soul, He (glory be to Him) arranged these two attributes in this way. However, the intended meanings sometimes Allah the Exalted makes manifest to His servant as a gift and honor, and sometimes He conceals them to show His servant's inability and deficiency, and then He makes them manifest to him at another time, if he is sincere in supplication, in showing need and humility, and persists in seeking; or [He reveals them] to someone other than him who is lesser in knowledge and weaker in insight and understanding. When you reflect on this book of mine, it will become clear to you that many verses were explained by great scholars in a way other than what is definitely intended by them. So a person, when something remains hidden from him, should say: "I do not know," and should not think that any part of this noble Book was arranged for the sake of verse-endings (fawāṣil). That is a matter unbefitting the speech of Allah the Exalted. The Prophet (ﷺ) criticized sajʿ (rhymed prose), because the one who uses sajʿ makes words his main concern, so he turns meanings around them and makes them follow the words, and so the word may fall short of conveying the meaning. Al-Bukhārī in al-Ṭibb and others in his Ṣaḥīḥ, Muslim in al-Diyāt, Abū Dāwūd, al-Nasāʾī and others narrated from Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ruled concerning a fetus killed in its mother's womb that its blood-money is a ghurrah, a male or female slave. The one against whom the ruling was given said: 'How shall I pay compensation for one who neither drank nor ate, nor spoke nor cried out? Such a one should be disregarded (yuṭall).' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'This is one of the brothers of the soothsayers,' because of his sajʿ which he rhymed." In another narration: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Sajʿ like the sajʿ of the bedouins."

That is, Allah knows best, because if his attention had been on the meaning and its correctness, he would not have needed this sajʿ, to say: "How shall I pay compensation for one who has no life?" And if he had intended sajʿ and refining the meaning, he would have come with something indicating the negation of life, which he made the focus of his ruling; for what he said does not entail its negation. And had he been bound by correctness, negating speech would have sufficed without negating crying out. So it is established by this that it revolves with the embellishment of the wording, whether the meaning is correct or not. And it would occur to any intelligent person that the Prophet (ﷺ) would not dispraise sajʿ while himself using it and intending it in the Qur'an or in the Sunnah; and if that were the case, they would have quickly rejected it. The authors of the conquests of lands mentioned, regarding the conquest of Mukrān in the lands of Fārs, that al-Ḥakam ibn ʿAmr, when he conquered it, sent the one-fifths (of the booty) with Ṣuḥār al-ʿAbdī. When he came to ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, he asked him about Mukrān, and no one came to him without ʿUmar asking him about the route by which he had come. He said: "O Commander of the Believers! It is a land whose plains are mountains, its water is a trickle, its fruit is inferior dates, its enemy is a brave one, its good is little, its evil is long, the much there is little, the little there is lost, and what lies beyond it is worse than it." ʿUmar said: "Are you a rhymester (sajjāʿ) or a reporter?" He said: "No, rather a reporter." He said: "By Allah! No army of mine shall invade it so long as I am obeyed." So al-Fārūq made sajʿ a counterpart to reporting (khabar). This indicates that restriction to it is a fault, because it undermines the benefit or the full benefit. Perhaps he was considered a reporter only because he departed from sajʿ at the end of his speech and repeated the word "little," so it was as he had supposed. For had he intended sajʿ, he could have said: "And the much there is humble, the little there is lost and weary, and what lies beyond it is worse than it in the most upright statement." Allah (glory be to Him) has also negated from this glorious Qur'an directing attention to sajʿ, just as He negated poetry from it. For He (Exalted) said: ﴿And it is not the word of a poet; little do you believe﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah: 41] ﴿Nor the word of a soothsayer; little do you remember﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah: 42]. Just as the word of the poet is its bringing speech in measured form, so the word of the soothsayer is its bringing speech in rhymed prose (masjūʿ), and the Qur'an is neither of these. If either of the two matters occurs in it, it is not intended or relied upon for itself; rather, the meaning is arranged in it in the most complete manner, and so it is brought for that reason. Then it becomes clear that it is not intended, since it departs from it in many places, through a context that has no counterpart in wording, because the intended meanings are complete there. Thus it is known with certainty that this is not intended at all, for such a thing would not be accepted even by the least of the rhymesters, but would be seen as incapacity and constriction in completing the harmony, and a deficiency, exalted is Allah far above that. Among what makes it certain to you that the arrangement of these two noble names in this way is not for the sake of observing verse-endings is His saying in Sūrat al-Ḥadīd: ﴿And We placed in the hearts of those who followed him tenderness and mercy﴾ [al-Ḥadīd: 27]. And it will come, Allah willing, in Sūrat Ṭā-Hā, from al-Fakhr al-Rāzī and al-Qāḍī Abū Bakr al-Bāqillānī, the prohibition of regarding sajʿ in the Glorious Book, transmitted from all of the Ashʿarīs. When you reflect on the verse-endings, in their occurrence sometimes in abundance and sometimes [in scarcity, and sometimes] completely absent, and in every verse there comes an ending that does not agree with the others, you will know that this school of thought is the correct one, especially the end of Sūrat "Iqraʾ." And when you reflect on the books of the scholars of enumeration (ahl al-ʿadad), you will master the knowledge of this basis. And when you reflect on what I have said in this regard in my book "Maṣāʿid al-Naẓar lil-Sharrāf ʿalā Maqāṣid al-Suwar," no doubt will remain for you regarding any part of this. So beware of inclining to this view, lest you fall into a grave matter while you are unaware.

Allah (glory be to Him) presented this verse in the manner of one addressing them gently, removing the doubt they had by means of an oath, as if He said: [What is wrong with you that] you turn away from his lofty presence and his exalted qualities! By Allah, there has certainly come to you—to the end of it,

Then He turned to him (ﷺ), consoling him and countering their aversion: if they turn away, then he should turn away from them and disassociate himself from them, turning toward the surah that commands disassociation from every opponent. He said, basing it on the advice contained in this verse, whose meaning no sensible person doubts: ﴿But if they turn away﴾, that is, they strive to force their original natures (fitar) [to conform to something else], or they turn their backs on you, departing in the manner mentioned or otherwise, after having been advised by this verse. ﴿Then say﴾, [that is] seeking help from Allah [entrusting the matter to Him]: ﴿Sufficient for me﴾, that is, my Sufficer. Al-Rummani said: it derives from ḥisāb (reckoning), because He, exalted is His praise, gives according to the measure of sufficiency that suffices one without anyone else, and increases His blessings beyond any limit or end, since His blessings are everlasting and His favors continuous. ﴿Allah﴾, that is, the Supreme King, who has no equal. He is sufficient precisely because ﴿there is no god but Him﴾; so there is no counterpart to Him, no one can repel His command, and no one can revoke His judgment.

Since the proof has been established that He has no equal, it is necessary to confine one's hopes to Him (p-61). So He said: ﴿In Him﴾, that is, Him alone, ﴿I have put my trust﴾, because His command is effective over everything. ﴿And He is the Lord﴾, that is, the Owner, the Originator, and the Governor of the [Ṣ]. [Since the context is one of dominance and majesty, through disassociation from the disbelievers and sufficiency for the righteous, the situation calls for greatness, more fitting, as in the verse of an-Naml, so He said]: ﴿of the Mighty Throne﴾, that is, the one encompassing all bodies, containing all celestial bodies [which, by the verse of the Throne (Kursi) and others, is established that its Lord is greater than it, since His greatness is absolute]. Thus nothing exists except that it is in His grip and within the circle of His dominion. And since He is All-Sufficient, I am free of whoever turns away from me and distances himself from me, whoever he may be, in every time and place. The end of the surah has thus embraced its beginning and shaken hands with its conclusion; what I understood of the secret of the shift in ﴿So travel﴾ [al-Tawbah: 2] and in ﴿So if you repent, it is better for you; but if you turn away, know that you cannot escape Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 3] is confirmed. [And Allah knows best.]
